chunks: From him, from Ali, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Zurara, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I have a debt on a man, and he intends to sell his house so that he may give it to me.' He said, and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'I advise you by God not to take it out from under the shadow of his head. I advise you by God not to take it out from under the shadow of his head.'

key_terms.أُعِيذُكَ: I advise you / I seek protection for you
key_terms.ظِلُّ رَأْسِهِ: shadow of his head (metaphor for shelter/dignity)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on seizing a debtor's home to pay off a debt?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) advises a creditor not to seize the debtor's house to settle a debt, using the metaphor of not removing the house from 'under the shadow of his head' to preserve the debtor's dignity and shelter. This ruling emphasizes ethical conduct in financial transactions and avoiding harshness towards debtors. The phrase 'shadow of his head' (zill ra'sihi) is interpreted by Shia scholars as the essential shelter or primary residence that provides security and status, suggesting that while debt is valid, the creditor should not deprive the debtor of their fundamental home or social standing.
